introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0760), Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections. All the questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections: SECTION A (1800 - 1922), questions 1 to 4; SECTION B (1922 - 1961), questions 5 to 8; SECTION C (1961 to present), questions 9 to 12.

Points : chaque question imprime « (25 marks) » et le sujet dit « All the questions carry equal marks » ; `points` vaut donc 25 pour chaque question. Aucun écart constaté entre les points imprimés.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les 12 questions) : filigrane et publicités gcerevision.com sans conséquence sur la lisibilité ; aucune question n'est coupée ni illisible. Page de garde vérifiée : « JUNE 2020 », ADVANCED LEVEL, History, Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, code 0760, trois heures.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire historiographique, sans accès à un manuel pendant la rédaction ; aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée. Les dates et les faits cités sont ceux de l'historiographie courante du Cameroun, mais n'ont pas pu être recoupés avec une source écrite : à relire par un historien avant publication.

Détails des expéditions allemandes cités de mémoire et à recouper : Zintgraff (1886-1891, Barombi, Bali, revers de 1891 dans les Grassfields), Kund et Tappenbeck (fin des années 1880), Morgen (fin des années 1880 - 1891), Zenker et Tappenbeck (station de Yaoundé, 1889), mort de von Gravenreuth près de Buea (1891), troupe de police de 1891, sociétés concessionnaires de 1898-1899, accords de 1893 (Grande-Bretagne) et 1894 (France). Traité duala du 12 juillet 1884 et proclamation du protectorat vers le 14 juillet 1884.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Account for the German penetration into the hinterland of Cameroon shortly after annexation in 1884.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Germany annexed the coast of Cameroon in July 1884: on 12 July the Duala kings, Bell and Akwa, signed a treaty with the agents of the Hamburg firm Woermann, and on about 14 July the German consul-general Gustav Nachtigal proclaimed a protectorate. This gave Germany a foothold on the coast, but not control of the interior, where the Duala and other coastal peoples acted as middlemen and where the resources were found. In the years after 1884 the Germans therefore pushed into the **hinterland**. The reasons were economic, strategic, political and scientific, and the methods were exploration, treaties, military force, stations and missionary and commercial activity.

**1. Reasons for the penetration**

- **Economic motives.** Germany wanted raw materials (palm oil and kernels, rubber, ivory, later cocoa, coffee and timber) and markets for its manufactures. The Duala and other coastal middlemen controlled the trade with the interior and took a large share of the profit. The German firms and the government wanted to **reach the producers directly and remove the middlemen's monopoly**. The coast also had little land for the plantations that German companies wished to establish, and the Mount Cameroon slopes and the forest belt attracted them.
- **Strategic and political motives.** Germany had to occupy and mark out the hinterland in order to make its claim valid against **Britain** (in the Niger area and in Nigeria) and **France** (in Gabon and the Congo), according to the principle of effective occupation agreed at the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885. A paper treaty on the coast was not enough: the Germans needed to extend their claims towards Lake Chad and the Benue and to reach the savanna trade routes before their rivals. The later agreements with Britain (1893) and with France (1894) drew boundaries that matched the areas they had reached.
- **Administrative and financial needs.** The colony had to pay for itself. Controlling the interior would permit taxation, labour recruitment and the founding of stations.
- **Scientific curiosity and prestige.** Explorers, geographers and officers wished to know the interior and win fame; the German public and the colonial societies supported expansion.
- **Missionary motives.** The Basel Mission (from 1886) and Catholic missions (from 1890) went inland in order to evangelise and found schools, and the government used them to reach the people.

**2. Methods of penetration**

- **Exploration and expeditions.** German officers and explorers led expeditions into the interior. Eugen Zintgraff led several expeditions between 1886 and 1891 into the Cameroon Grassfields (Bali, Bafut and Bamenda area) and set up a base at Barombi and a station at Bali; Lieutenants Kund and Tappenbeck explored the south in the late 1880s; Curt von Morgen explored the Adamawa region and the Sanaga country at the end of the decade; and Georg Zenker and Tappenbeck founded the Yaounde station in 1889, which became a centre for the occupation of the Beti country.
- **Treaties and alliances with local rulers.** Explorers made treaties and friendships with chiefs and used local rivalries. Zintgraff won the support of Fon Galega I of Bali Nyonga, whose warriors and porters helped his expeditions against other Grassfields chiefdoms. These alliances saved German resources.
- **Military force.** After a first period of peaceful exploration, the Germans used force against peoples who refused to submit or blocked the trade routes. The police troop formed in 1891 (the later Schutztruppe), made up mostly of African soldiers recruited from outside the area, including Hausa and men from Dahomey, was used against the Bakweri and other peoples, and several expeditions met serious resistance. In 1891 the German officer von Gravenreuth was killed in the fighting near Buea, and Zintgraff's expedition suffered a serious reverse in the Grassfields in the same year. The Germans responded with larger and better prepared expeditions in the 1890s.
- **Stations and posts.** Administrative and military stations (Yaounde, Barombi, Bali, Buea, later Bamenda, Ngaoundere and Garoua) were founded in the interior to hold the territory, collect taxes, recruit labour and open roads and paths.
- **Concessions and trading companies.** From the late 1890s the government gave huge concessions to companies (for example the Gesellschaft Sud-Kamerun and the Gesellschaft Nordwest-Kamerun), which opened up the interior to trade and rubber collection, and German firms also set up plantations.
- **Diplomacy with the European rivals.** The agreements with Britain and France in the early 1890s fixed the limits of the German claim in the hinterland.

**3. Obstacles.** The Duala fought to keep their middleman position, the peoples of the interior resisted, and distances, disease and lack of roads made progress slow. These were reasons why penetration was gradual.

**Conclusion.** German penetration into the hinterland after 1884 was explained mainly by the desire to reach the sources of raw materials without the coastal middlemen, by the need to secure the colony against the British and French, and by the wish for prestige and revenue. It was achieved by exploration, alliances, military force and the creation of stations, and it opened the way to full colonial occupation.
